title: Reachability and the input rank test

sections.figure_alt: Two arrows from the origin in clearly different directions.
sections.body_md:
Reachability asks whether the input can stir every state. For a linear system the answer is a rank. Line up \(B\), \(AB\), and so on until you have \(n\) blocks. If those columns span \(\mathbb{R}^n\), some input takes any state to any other state in finite time. If the rank \(r\) is short, only an \(r\)-dimensional subspace can be steered. The missing directions are modes the actuator never touches.

The same test is often called controllability. For the continuous-time models in this graph the two words name one rank condition. A coordinate change with an invertible \(T\) multiplies the matrix by \(T^{-1}\) and does not change the rank.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
The controllability matrix is
\[
\mathcal{C} = \begin{bmatrix} B & AB & \cdots & A^{n-1}B \end{bmatrix}.
\]
The pair is reachable when \(\mathrm{rank}\,\mathcal{C} = n\). For two states that is a nonzero determinant. In controllable canonical form the matrix is triangular and invertible, provided no factor was cancelled. A cancelled mode kept as an extra state is unreachable or unobservable.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Take \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -7.5 & -0.8 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1.6 \end{bmatrix}\). Then \(AB = \begin{bmatrix} 1.6 \\ -1.28 \end{bmatrix}\), and
\[
\mathcal{C} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1.6 \\ 1.6 & -1.28 \end{bmatrix}.
\]
The determinant is \(-2.56\). The columns point in different directions, so the pair is reachable. The \(1.6\) in \(B\) scales both columns and does not, by itself, decide the rank. A zero in the top entry of \(B\) is the usual companion pattern, not a missing direction.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: A nonzero \(B\) is not full rank. Two proportional columns still leave a hole. The determinant test is only for a square controllability matrix. In larger systems you count the rank. An unreachable mode is not automatically unstable, and state feedback cannot move it. Coordinate changes do not repair a short rank. And building a canonical form from a transfer function, which an earlier skill does, is not the same as testing the rank of a model you already have.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: State feedback \(u = -Kx\) can place every eigenvalue of \(A - BK\) only when the pair is reachable. The gain is a row you solve for so that the closed-loop characteristic polynomial matches a polynomial you chose. If the rank is short, the unreachable eigenvalues stay where \(A\) put them, no matter what \(K\) you write down.
